Final synthesis for human review:

The most defensible reading of Experiments 30 and 31 is that the persistence-layer codebase likely did converge qualitatively, but the experimental apparatus failed to register that convergence. The HIL’s assessment is supported by both the severity shift and the closure-path failures. Experiment 30 surfaced roughly 83 distinct bugs, including architectural and serious correctness issues, and 39 fixes were applied. Experiment 31 reviewed the same three files after those fixes and, after audit, the residual set collapsed to 13 verified findings: five in the harness, six low/medium edge cases, and two already fixed during the session. That is not the profile of a codebase still rich in high-severity defects. It is the profile of a system near PoC-ready closure whose instrumentation could not contract the finding set.

The failure mechanism is also clear. Experiment 31 had five independent closure failures: verified flags did not propagate back to canonical findings; locked rejections could be resurrected by autoimmune recovery; finding IDs were unstable across rounds; no model ever issued a formal CHALLENGE; and 58.3% of all findings were churn. Kappa at 0.619 shows the models were agreeing substantially. The problem was not lack of signal. The problem was that agreement had no reliable state transition path to closure. On that basis, Exp 31 should be interpreted as a measurement failure under probable code convergence, not as evidence that the codebase itself failed to converge.

For the next experiment, the consensus design is substantially settled. The communication protocol should be runner-centric, registry-driven, and state-owning. Models should not receive one another’s full prose. Each model should receive only the target artifact, the canonical finding registry summary, any messages explicitly addressed to it, evidence snippets for active contested findings, and round summary metrics. Full peer outputs should be archived for audit only. This change is justified directly by Exp 31’s transport waste: 1.26 million characters of output, only 2.9% cross-model reference overhead, and zero CHALLENGEs. The prior design paid huge context cost for almost no adversarial value.

The schema should be split in two. Models should emit only local proposals and verdicts. A minimal proposal schema is sufficient: FINDING_ID, SEVERITY, SCOPE, FLAW_CLASS, CLAIM, EVIDENCE, FOLLOW, FIX, CONFIDENCE. Verdicts should be separate objects, not overloaded into finding records. The runner should own the canonical registry and all global state, including CANONICAL_ID, STATUS, SEVERITY, SCOPE, FLAW_CLASS, ROOT_CAUSE, CLAIM, EVIDENCE, FOLLOW, FIX, SOURCE_IDS, ROUND_OPENED, LAST_TOUCHED, and CLOSURE_BASIS. This is required because the broken VERIFIED/closed path in Exp 31 demonstrates that model-emitted global status is the wrong ownership boundary. FOLLOW-before-FIX should be enforced mechanically by runner validation, since prompt-only instruction failed completely in Exp 31.

The recommended reviewer set is three active top-level models every round—CC2, Codex, and Gemini—plus one reserve reviewer, ChatGPT, invoked only for escalations and final residual audit. That recommendation follows the artifact, not taste. The three selected models are from independent families and were also the most efficient by findings per kilochar: CC2 at 0.40, Gemini at 0.31, Codex at 0.29. ChatGPT and DeepSeek were least efficient at 0.23 and 0.22. Keeping all five active every round is not justified by the data and would repeat the communication burden that dominated Exp 31. CC2 should additionally run an internal three-way split—Structural, Semantic, and Integration—with strict pre-registry deduplication and an overlap kill-switch if internal duplicate rate exceeds 30% for two consecutive rounds. That preserves the strongest reviewer’s breadth without increasing top-level coordination cost.

The round budget should be eight rounds by default, with conditional extension to ten. Stop checks should begin at Round 6. The extension decision should be taken at the end of Round 8, not earlier, because the stop rule requires two consecutive rounds of stable state. This budget is the best fit to the observed novelty tail. In Exp 31, novel findings dropped sharply after the Round 7 interventions; if those interventions are present from Round 0, the drop should shift earlier. An 8-to-10 round budget preserves enough room to observe stabilization while avoiding the obvious tail waste of a 15-round default.

The main unresolved disagreement is gamma. The evidence does not support gamma > 0.5 as a hard termination gate in this environment. Exp 31 ended at gamma = 0.106 despite strong qualitative evidence of closure. Even after stripping churn, CC2’s recomputation gives novel-only gamma = 0.38 over the full 15-round run. Exp 30 shows the opposite instability, starting above 0.5 and then declining steadily to 0.320. That means gamma is informative as trend telemetry but unreliable as a binary veto in short, stateful code-review experiments. I therefore recommend a state-based non-compensatory stop rule and telemetry-only gamma.

The stop rule should be: terminate when all of the following hold for two consecutive rounds, with checks beginning at Round 6: there are zero open unique target-code findings with severity CRITICAL or HIGH; the number of new novel target-code findings of any severity is at most two; and no finding remains in pending resolution or contested for more than one full subsequent round. Gamma_novel_target, kappa_agreement, immune_rejection_rate, and total open target-code findings should still be logged every round, but as diagnostics rather than hard gates. The reserve reviewer should be triggered whenever a canonical finding remains open and contested for more than one full subsequent round after first challenge, or when canonicalization remains unstable across rounds even without an explicit CHALLENGE.

On convergence prediction, the safest agreed forecast is not that gamma will cross 0.5, but that operational convergence will be reached by Round 8 to 10 under the repaired protocol while gamma likely remains below 0.5. My best point estimate for stop-time gamma is about 0.33, with a 90% confidence interval of 0.20 to 0.45. That forecast assumes the Round-0 protocol repairs actually eliminate the five documented instrumentation failures, that the residual defect pool is mostly non-target or low-severity as the HIL audit indicates, and that reviewer behavior changes materially once AGREE/CHALLENGE/EXTEND and mandatory merge are active from the start. It would be falsified if the repaired experiment still discovers multiple new CRITICAL/HIGH target-code issues after Round 8, or if gamma exceeds 0.5 early while blocker state remains open—either outcome would show that our current mapping between Duane dynamics and canonical finding state is still wrong.

The dissenting view is narrow but important. CC2 argues gamma should remain in the hard stop gate, with the threshold lowered to 0.35 instead of 0.5. That position has a real rationale: gamma can act as protection against false lulls. The counterargument, which I find better supported by the artifact, is that once canonical open-blocker state, novelty, and contest persistence are tracked correctly, gamma no longer carries enough unique decision value to justify veto power. The evidence in favor of hard-gated gamma is mostly calibration logic and simulation; the evidence against it is direct observation from both experiments. Additional data that would resolve this dispute is straightforward: run the repaired protocol on the same artifact class for multiple trials and record whether gamma threshold crossing consistently coincides with state closure. If it does, gamma can be promoted later. If it does not, it should remain advisory permanently.

Definitive stance: treat Exp 31 as probable code convergence masked by broken measurement, run the next experiment as a validation of the repaired protocol, and use a state-based stop rule with gamma as telemetry only.
